source_text: Οἷος οὖν τις σπινθὴρ ἐνσκήψας μέσῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἡμῶν, ἀνήπτετό τε καὶ ἐξεριπίζετο, ὅ, τε πρὸς τὸν ἁπάντων ὑπὸ κάλλους ἀρρήτου ἐπακτικώτατον αὐτὸν λόγον τὸν ἱερὸν τὸν ἐρασμιώτατον. καὶ ὁ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα τόνδε τὸν αὐτοῦ φίλον καὶ προήγορον, ἔρως, ᾧ μάλιστα τετρωμένος, ἁπάντων τῶν δοκούντων ἡμῖν προσήκειν πραγμάτων ἢ μαθημάτων, τῶν τε ἄλλων καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν καλῶν μου νόμων, ἀμελεῖν ἐπείσθην. πατρίδος τε καὶ οἰκείων τῶν τε παρόντων ἐνταῦθα, καὶ οἷς ἀπεδημήσαμεν. ἓν δέ μοι φίλον ἦν καὶ ἀγαπώμενον, φιλοσοφία τε καὶ ὁ ταύτης καθηγεμὼν οὗτος ὁ θεῖος ἄνθρωπος. καὶ συνεδέθη ἡ ψυχὴ Ἰωνάθαν Δαβίδ. τοῦτο ἀνέγνων μὲν ὕστερον ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασιν. ἔπαθον δὲ πρότερον οὐκ ἧττον ἐναργῶς, ἢ εἴρηται, καί τοι γε ἐναργέστατα κεχρησμῳδημένων. οὐ γὰρ συνεδέθη ἁπλῶς Ἰωνάθαν Δαβίδ. αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ κυριώτατα, ψυχή, ταῦθ᾽ ἅπερ οὐδὲ χωρισθέντων τῶν φαινομένων καὶ βλεπομένων ἀνθρώπων, χωρισθῆναι καὶ αὐτὰ μηχανῇ τινι καταναγκασθήσεται, ἄκοντα μὲν, οὐδαμῶς. ψυχὴ γὰρ ἐλεύθερον καὶ οὐκ ἐγκατάκλειστον οὐδενὶ τρόπῳ, οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐν οἰκίσκῳ καθείρξας τηρῇς. καὶ γὰρ εἶναι πέφυκε τόν γε πρῶτον λόγον, οὗπερ ἂν ὁ νοῦς ᾖ. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐν τῷ οἰκίσκῳ σοι εἶναι δοκεῖ, κατὰ δεύτερόν τινα λόγον ἐνταῦθα εἶναι φαντάζεται. οὐδαμῶς εἶναι ἐκεῖ διὰ τοῦτο κεκωλυμένη, οὗπερ ἂν εἶναι βουληθῇ. μᾶλλον δὲ πάντῃ πάντως ἐκεῖ μόνον εἶναι καὶ δυναμένη καὶ πιστευθεῖσα ἂν εἰκότως, οὗπερ ἂν καὶ πρὸς ὃ δὴ τὰ μόνης αὐτῆς ἴδια κατ᾽ αὐτὴν ἔργα ᾖ. οὐκοῦν περιφανέστατα τοῦθ᾽ ὅπερ ἔπαθον βραχυτάταις λέξεσιν ἐδήλωσε, τὴν ψυχὴν Ἰωνάθαν συνδεδέσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ Δαβίδ. ταῦθ᾽ ἅπερ ἄκοντα μὲν οὐδαμῶς, ὡς ἔφην, χωρισθῆναι ἐκνικηθήσεται, ἑκόντα δὲ οὐ ῥᾳδίως θελήσει. οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῷ χείρονι, οἶμαι, ὄντι πολυτρόπῳ καὶ εὐκολωτέρῳ μεταβουλεύεσθαι, ἡ τῆς ἀναλύσεως τῶν ἱερῶν τῶν φιλίων τούτων δεσμῶν ἐξουσία. ἐφ᾽ ᾧπερ οὐδὲ τὸ καταδήσασθαι ἐγίνετο τὴν ἀρχὴν μόνῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ τῷ κρείττονι ὄντι μονίμῳ, καὶ οὐκ εὐπίστῳ, ἐφ᾽ ᾧπερ καὶ κατεργάσασθαι τοὺς δεσμοὺς καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦτο ἅμμα μᾶλλον ἦν. συνεδέθη γοῦν καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θείου λόγου, οὐχ ἡ ψυχὴ Δαβίδ, τῇ ψυχῇ Ἰωνάθαν. ἔμπαλιν δὲ ἡ τοῦ χείρονος ψυχὴ τοῦτο παθοῦσα συνδεομένη λέγεται τῇ ψυχῇ Δαβίδ. οὐ γὰρ τὸ κρεῖττον αὔταρκες ὄν, ἕλοιτο ἂν τῷ αὐτοῦ συνδεδέσθαι χείρονι. ἀλλὰ τὸ χεῖρον ἐπικουρίας δεόμενον τῆς παρὰ τοῦ βελτίονος, συνδεθὲν τῷ κρείττονι προσηρτῆσθαι ἐχρῆν. ἵνα τὸ μὲν, μένον ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, μηδεμιᾶς ἀπολάβῃ βλάβης ἐκ τῆς πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον κοινωνίας. τὸ δ᾽ ἄτακτον ἐξ αὐτοῦ καταδεθὲν καὶ συναρμοσθὲν τῷ κρείττονι, μηδὲν βλέψαν ταῖς ἀνάγκαις τῶν δεσμῶν πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον ἐκνικηθῇ. διὸ καὶ κατεργάζεσθαι μὲν τοὺς δεσμοὺς, τοῦ διαφέροντος, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ τοῦ ἥττονος ἦν. συνδεῖσθαι δὲ τοῦ χείρονος, ὡς μηδ᾽ ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν πως, ἀπολελύσθαι τῶν δεσμῶν. Τοιαύταις τισὶν ἀνάγκαις Δαβὶδ οὗτος συσφιγξάμενος ἡμᾶς ἔχει, νῦν τε καὶ ἐξ ἐκείνου, οὐδ᾽ εἰ βουλοίμεθα τῶν δεσμῶν αὐτοῦ λελύσθαι δυναμένους. οὐ τοίνυν καὶ εἰ ἀποδημήσαιμεν, ἀνήσει τὰς ψυχὰς ἡμῶν κατὰ τὸ θεῖον γράμμα ἔχων οὕτως συνδεδεμένας.
thought_title: The spark of love: bound like Jonathan to David
orientation: Love for the Word and for Origen binds Gregory to him, as Jonathan's soul was bound to David's.
pass_a_gloss: As some spark falling into the middle of our soul, was kindled and fanned the [love] toward the most attractive of all by unspeakable beauty, the Word himself, the holy, the most lovely; and the love toward this man, his friend and advocate; by which most wounded, I was persuaded to neglect all the affairs or studies that seemed to belong to us, the others and even my fine laws; [and] homeland and kin, those present here and those from whom we went abroad. One thing was dear and beloved to me: philosophy and its guide, this divine man. And the soul of Jonathan was bound to David [1 Sam 18:1]. This I read later in the sacred writings; but I experienced it earlier, not less vividly than it is said, though most vividly oracled. For Jonathan was not simply bound to David, but the most proper things, soul [print abbreviated ψυχή; Koetschau ψυχή], which, even when the visible and seen men are separated, will not be compelled by any device to be separated; unwilling, in no way. For soul is a free thing and in no way shut in, not even if you shut it up in a little room and keep it. For it is by nature, in the first account, wherever the mind is; and if it seems to you to be in the little room, by a second account it is imagined to be there; in no way hindered by this from being where it wishes; rather wholly and entirely both able and rightly to be believed to be only there where and toward which are the works proper to it alone. Therefore most plainly it declared in shortest words what I experienced: the soul of Jonathan to have been bound to the soul of David. These, unwilling, as I said, will in no way be overcome to be separated, and willing will not easily want it. For not with the worse, I think, which is many-turned and readier to change counsel, is the power of loosing these sacred friendly bonds, with whom not even the binding lay alone at the start, but with the better, which is abiding and not easily persuaded, with whom rather lay the making of the bonds and this sacred knot. At any rate by the divine word too it is not the soul of David that was bound to the soul of Jonathan; but contrariwise the soul of the worse, having experienced this, is said to be bound to the soul of David. For the better, being self-sufficient, would not choose to be bound to its inferior; but the worse, needing help from the better, being bound to the better had to hang upon it; so that the one, remaining by itself, receive no harm from the fellowship with the worse; and the disordered in itself, bound down and fitted to the better, [print μηδὲν βλέψαν, doubtful; Koetschau μηδὲν βλάψαν 'having harmed nothing'], by the constraints of the bonds be overcome toward the better. Hence making the bonds belonged to the superior, not the lesser; being bound to the worse, so as not to have power somehow to be loosed from the bonds. With such constraints this David, having bound us tight, holds us, now and since then, not able, even if we wished, to be loosed from his bonds. Nor then, even if we go abroad, will he let go our souls, holding them thus bound together according to the divine writing.

pass_b_english: Like a spark dropping into the middle of our soul, love was kindled there and fanned into flame: love for the holy Word himself, the most lovely, who by his unspeakable beauty is the most winning of all, and love for this man, his friend and advocate. Wounded deeply by this love, I was persuaded to neglect all the affairs and studies that seemed to concern us, among them even my fine laws, and to neglect my homeland and my family, both those who are here with me and those we left when we went abroad. One thing alone was dear to me and loved: philosophy, and this divine man who is its guide.

“And the soul of Jonathan was bound to David” (1 Samuel 18:1). I read this only later in the holy Scriptures, but I had felt it before, no less vividly than it is told there, though the inspired words there put it most vividly. For it was not simply Jonathan who was bound to David, but what is most truly theirs, their souls: things which, even when the men who appear and are seen are parted, will not be forced apart by any device, not against their will at any rate. For the soul is a free thing and cannot be shut in by any means, not even if you lock it up and guard it in a little cell. By nature it is, in the primary sense, wherever the mind is; and if it seems to you to be in the cell, it is pictured as being there in a secondary sense. This in no way prevents it from being wherever it wishes to be. Rather, it can be, and would rightly be believed to be, wholly and in every way only there where the activities that belong to it alone are found, and toward which they are directed.

So the text showed most plainly, in the fewest words, what I experienced: that the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David (1 Samuel 18:1). These souls, as I said, will never be overpowered into separation against their will, and they will not easily wish it of their own accord. For the power to undo these sacred bonds of friendship does not lie, I think, with the worse party, who is changeable and more easily changes his mind (the binding did not lie with him alone at the beginning either), but with the better, who is steadfast and not easily won over, and to whom it belonged rather to make the bonds and to tie this sacred knot. At any rate, in the divine word too it is not the soul of David that was bound to the soul of Jonathan; on the contrary, it is the soul of the worse, which underwent this, that is said to be bound to the soul of David. For the better, being sufficient in itself, would not choose to be bound to what is worse than itself; but the worse, needing help from the better, had to be bound to the better and to hang upon it. In this way the one, remaining as it was, would take no harm from its fellowship with the worse, while the other, disordered in itself, once bound and fitted to the better, would be won over to the better by the constraints of the bonds without doing it any harm. So making the bonds belonged to the superior, not to the inferior; being bound belonged to the worse, so that it should have no power in any way to be set free from the bonds. With constraints such as these this David holds us bound fast, now and ever since that time, and even if we wished, we could not be loosed from his bonds. Nor, then, even if we go away, will he let go of our souls, which, as the divine Scripture says, he holds so bound together.
notes: Scripture: the quotation 'the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David' is 1 Samuel 18:1 (LXX 1 Kingdoms 18:1; this verse is missing from some Greek witnesses, which omit 1 Samuel 17:55-18:5, but Gregory plainly read it). Cited at the first quotation and at the full restatement; the later echoes in the argument are left uncited to avoid repetition. 'Most winning' (ἐπακτικώτατον, literally 'most drawing') by unspeakable beauty: a possible echo of John 12:32 is too loose to cite. 'Lock it up in a little cell' may echo Demosthenes, On the Crown 97 (Koetschau's note); not Scripture, not cited. Readings: the print's ἐξεριπίζετο ('fanned into flame') is followed (Koetschau ἐξεκαίετο). The print puts a full stop after ἀμελεῖν ἐπείσθην, but the genitives πατρίδος τε καὶ οἰκείων depend on ἀμελεῖν, so they are joined to that clause, as in Koetschau. Doubtful readings: ψυχή (abbreviated in the print) rendered 'their souls'; οὐκ εὐπίστῳ (print) rendered 'not easily won over', which also fits Koetschau's εὐσείστῳ ('not easily shaken'); ἀπολάβῃ (print) and ἀπολαύῃ (Koetschau) give the same sense, 'take no harm'; μηδὲν βλέψαν (print, doubtful and hard to construe) rendered with Koetschau's μηδὲν βλάψαν, 'without doing it any harm'. Gregory casts himself as the 'worse' Jonathan and Origen as David; 'the Word' is the divine Word and is capitalized. The print reads ταῖς ἀνάγκαις τῶν δεσμῶν (plural, as Koetschau), so the English says 'the constraints of the bonds'.
